records.title: [Agent] Prove agentic execution with recursive v3 composition
Build a deterministic weighted scheduler for portfolio planning order
records.body:
## Outcome

Given a large evolving ticket portfolio, deterministically recommend which single ticket should be planned next and explain why. Optimize planning order separately from implementation order so plans are produced when they unlock value without becoming stale before execution.

## Graph model

Represent a versioned portfolio snapshot as a directed graph:

* Nodes: exact tracker issue revision plus project/repository context and planning state (`untriaged`, `discovery-needed`, `plan-ready`, `planned`, `stale-plan`, `implemented`, or terminal).
* Hard edges: explicit `blockedBy`/`blocks`, required contract or migration sequencing, and human-approved dependency edges. Hard edges constrain topological eligibility.
* Soft edges: related work, shared contracts/packages/files, conflict surface, information dependencies, and model-proposed sequencing. Soft edges affect score only and retain evidence/confidence/provenance.
* Model-inferred edges begin as caller/model claims and cannot silently become hard blockers.

Detect strongly connected components. Any hard-edge cycle is a human escalation; the scheduler must not invent an arbitrary order.

## Deterministic planning score

For each node on the eligible topological frontier, calculate a versioned integer/fixed-point score from trusted configurable weights:

* business priority and deadline pressure;
* downstream unblock reach and critical-path contribution;
* risk-reduction value;
* information gain for later tickets;
* requirement and contract readiness;
* expected planning effort/token cost;
* implementation volatility and plan-staleness risk;
* shared-file/conflict cost with active work;
* dependency confidence and unresolved-human-decision penalty.

Use a documented WSJF/critical-path-inspired formula with normalized bounded inputs. Do not claim mathematical optimality under uncertain estimates; call the result the deterministic recommended order. Stable ties resolve by immutable project/ticket identity, never insertion order or model preference.

## Planning versus implementation order

* Planning may move ahead of implementation only within a configured staleness horizon and dependency-confidence threshold.
* Tickets with unstable prerequisites may receive bounded discovery work but not a falsely final implementation plan.
* A merged contract, changed dependency, ticket revision, policy version, or repository base can mark dependent plans stale and trigger reranking.
* Recompute after each material plan, dependency, implementation, cancellation, priority, or policy change.
* Enforce a planning WIP limit; the first implementation supports one active planning target at a time.

## Inputs and authority

* Linear/tracker relations and human decisions are authoritative only through their configured adapter/receipt boundary.
* Repository impact and plan metadata come from exact cited research generated by Zkrausman/pith#48.
* Candidate branches, wiki content, environment variables, and ad hoc model prose cannot alter weights or hard dependencies.
* Weights, formula version, bounds, staleness horizon, and tie-break rules live in versioned trusted portfolio policy.

## Outputs

Emit a bounded machine-readable schedule containing:

* portfolio snapshot identity and formula/policy version;
* eligible frontier and blocked/cycle diagnostics;
* recommended next ticket and ordered alternatives;
* component scores, dependency path, sensitivity, and human-readable explanation;
* low-confidence or weight-sensitive ordering warnings;
* stale plans and discovery-only recommendations;
* exact input issue/repository revisions.

## Acceptance

* A fixed graph and policy always produce byte-identical order and explanation data.
* Hard dependencies are never violated even when a blocked ticket has the highest raw value.
* Hard cycles escalate with the exact cycle; no order is emitted for the affected component.
* Soft/model-inferred edges influence rank without becoming authority.
* High downstream-unblock value can outrank a locally attractive leaf ticket.
* High volatility/staleness cost prevents planning a distant unstable ticket too early.
* Stable tie-breaking is independent of input enumeration order.
* Small weight perturbation that changes the winner is surfaced as low sensitivity confidence.
* Updating or merging a prerequisite deterministically reranks affected tickets and marks stale plans.
* A representative snapshot containing [AIDEV-132](https://linear.app/geltagentictrading/issue/AIDEV-132/build-isolated-cited-sensitivity-scanned-ticket-retrospectives) through Zkrausman/pith#48 produces an inspectable recommended sequence without planning all tickets simultaneously.

## Non-goals

* Autonomous priority changes, ticket mutation, planning execution, implementation dispatch, or merge.
* Claiming a globally optimal schedule from uncertain human/model estimates.
* Replacing human portfolio decisions; operators may select another eligible node with a recorded r

<!-- kast-performance-audit:KPA-000 -->

Requirement key: `KPA-000`

## Outcome

Coordinate independent characterization, observability, and defect-repair lanes, then converge on exact-head performance and full-surface audits.

## Audit basis

Observed during the hermetic audit of [PR #569](https://github.com/amichne/kast/pull/569) at exact head `60dcf69d0431d38d8a2bb5476ee349a9f796829b`.

The exact-head hermetic audit found reliable bounded execution alongside distinct measurement, performance, output-contract, runtime-stop, stdin, and packaging defects.

## Requirement

| ID | Normative requirement | Acceptance evidence | Verification | Depends on |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `KPA-000` | The delivery graph MUST keep measurement independent from known repairs and MUST converge only through verified post-fix audit gates. | Native parent and blocked-by graph readback, an acyclic dependency graph, and the expected ready frontier. | API, E2E | None |

## Relationships

- Parent: None
- Blocked by: None
- Contains:
- [Define a reproducible performance audit evidence contract](https://github.com/amichne/kast/issues/571)
- [Capture the pinned pre-fix public tooling baseline](https://github.com/amichne/kast/issues/572)
- [Make profiling settings emit usable runtime artifacts](https://github.com/amichne/kast/issues/573)
- [Correlate public CLI requests with backend trace phases](https://github.com/amichne/kast/issues/574)
- [Create a comparative audit suite without setting scale policy](https://github.com/amichne/kast/issues/575)
- [Remove the Unix socket handler cleanup lock convoy](https://github.com/amichne/kast/issues/576)
- [Scale derived topology without rescanning every edge per community](https://github.com/amichne/kast/issues/577)
- [Bound graph topology and community output for agent consumption](https://github.com/amichne/kast/issues/578)
- [Make runtime stop report the observed terminal state](https://github.com/amichne/kast/issues/579)
- [Honor machine output selection for every CLI failure](https://github.com/amichne/kast/issues/580)
- [Accept declaration input with a conventional trailing newline](https://github.com/amichne/kast/issues/581)
- [Package development bundles for the detected host platform](https://github.com/amichne/kast/issues/582)
- [Characterize post-fix performance with the comparative suite](https://github.com/amichne/kast/issues/583)
- [Reindex and audit the complete public tooling surface after fixes](https://github.com/amichne/kast/issues/584)

The native GitHub parent and dependency graph is authoritative. These links mirror it for readers and agents.

## Existing scale-policy boundary

[Create a comparative audit suite without setting scale policy](https://github.com/amichne/kast/issues/575) does not define supported limits. [Publish scale profiles and enforce bounded deterministic work](https://github.com/amichne/kast/issues/541) remains authoritative for normative scale targets and enforcement. This graph supplies observed and comparative evidence without adding a false dependency on that policy issue.

## Expected ownership

- Tracker state only.

Exact allowed writes MUST be narrowed in `.agent/TASK.md` before implementation and MUST NOT silently expand beyond this ownership.

## RED-GREEN evidence

| Phase | Required record |
|---|---|
| Baseline | Read back the live issue graph before any relationship mutation. Record exact source state and known unrelated failures. |
| RED | Not applicable: this is an orchestration parent, not a production implementation issue. Infrastructure failure is not RED. |
| GREEN | Every child and direct prerequisite reads back with the intended native relationship. |
| Regression | Recompute the DAG and ready frontier after every relationship or completion change. |
| Delivery | No implementation pull request is required for this orchestration parent; retain live graph readback evidence. |

## Completion rule

Complete only when every child is complete and the native relationship graph still matches the linked mirror and remains acyclic.

## Non-goals

- Implement any child outcome in this issue.
- Define supported scale targets or enforcement policy owned by [Publish scale profiles and enforce bounded deterministic work](https://github.com/amichne/kast/issues/541).
- Treat qualified graph or relationship evidence as complete.

records.title: Rule Performance Profiler
records.body:
# Rule Performance Profiler

## Summary
Add per-invocation profiling that produces a **call tree** across rule dependency
chains and **exports to a standard flame-graph format** (speedscope / Chrome
trace), going beyond the aggregate counters we already collect.

## What exists today
- `RuleMetrics` (`RoslynRules/Models/RuleMetrics.cs`) — thread-safe, per-rule
  **aggregate** counters: `EvalCount`, `FailureCount`, `AverageExecutionTimeMs`,
  `FailureRatePercent`, `LastExecuted`, `TotalTicks`. Exposed via `Rule.Metrics`.
- Per-rule lifecycle events (`Rule.Events.cs`): `OnRuleExecuting`
  (cancelable) and `OnRuleExecuted` (`Result`, `Elapsed`, `Exception`).
- Dependency structure: `Rule.DependsOnRuleId` / `Rule.ParentRuleId`, plus the
  topological sort and `RuleGraphVisualizer`.

## Gap
`RuleMetrics` is aggregate-only — you can see that rule X averaged 0.4 ms over
1,000 evals, but not **where a single evaluation spent its time across the
dependency chain**, and there is no export a flame-graph tool can open.

## Proposed design
A lightweight, **opt-in** profiling scope that records one node per rule
invocation (start ticks, duration, failed, rule Id, parent invocation), assembles
a call tree using the existing `DependsOnRuleId` / `ParentRuleId` links, and
serializes it.

- Opt-in so there is zero cost on the hot path when unused (aggregate
  `RuleMetrics` recording stays as-is).
- Leaf granularity is **one rule** — we compile each expression to a single IL
  delegate, so we cannot profile *inside* an expression. Call this out explicitly.
- Ship exporters, not a GUI: **speedscope JSON** (primary) and optionally
  Chrome `chrome://tracing` JSON. Users open the file in existing viewers.

### Public API sketch
```csharp
// Opt-in scope; disposing stops capture and yields the tree.
using (var session = ProfilerSession.Start(compiledWorkflow))
{
    compiledWorkflow.Execute(parameters);      // one or many runs
    ProfileReport report = session.Report();

    report.WriteSpeedscope("profile.speedscope.json");
    // report.WriteChromeTrace("profile.trace.json"); // optional

    foreach (RuleProfile p in report.Rules)        // aggregate roll-up
        Console.WriteLine($"{p.Description}: self={p.SelfMs}ms total={p.TotalMs}ms calls={p.Calls}");
}
```

```csharp
public sealed class ProfileReport
{
    public IReadOnlyList<ProfileNode> Roots { get; }   // call tree
    public IReadOnlyList<RuleProfile> Rules { get; }   // per-rule roll-up
    public void WriteSpeedscope(string path);
    public string ToSpeedscopeJson();
}

public sealed class ProfileNode
{
    public Guid RuleId { get; }
    public string Description { get; }
    public double DurationMs { get; }
    public bool Failed { get; }
    public IReadOnlyList<ProfileNode> Children { get; }
}
```

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `ProfilerSession.Start(...)` captures every rule invocation within its scope
      with duration and failed flag; no capture occurs when a session is not active.
- [ ] Call tree correctly nests children under the rule they depend on
      (`DependsOnRuleId` / `ParentRuleId`); independent rules appear as siblings/roots.
- [ ] `WriteSpeedscope` output opens cleanly in https://speedscope.app.
- [ ] Per-rule roll-up reports `SelfMs`, `TotalMs`, and `Calls`.
- [ ] Works for `Execute` and `ExecuteParallel*` (parallel invocations attributed
      to the correct rule; document any ordering caveats).
- [ ] Benchmark showing ~zero overhead when no session is active.
- [ ] Unit tests + a `Demo` sample that emits a `.speedscope.json`.

## Non-goals
- No bundled/graphical flame-graph UI — export only.
- No sub-expression (intra-IL) profiling; one rule is the smallest unit.

## Open questions
- Overhead model for `ExecuteParallel*` — per-thread buffers merged on `Report()`?
- Should aggregate `RuleMetrics` optionally feed a "no-tree" summary export too?

records.title: PRD01-SUB15-PLAN01: Implement Backoffice Organizational Foundation
records.body:
## Overview

Implement foundational components of the Backoffice module including company master data management, organizational hierarchy (branches, departments, cost centers) with closure table pattern for efficient queries (< 100ms for 1000+ entities), and core data structures supporting all transactional modules.

**Related Plan:** [PRD01-SUB15-PLAN01](https://github.com/azaharizaman/laravel-erp/blob/main/docs/plan/PRD01-SUB15-PLAN01-implement-organizational-foundation.md)

## Key Features

- Company master data (registration, tax IDs, addresses, bank accounts)
- Organizational hierarchy with closure table pattern
- Branch/office management with multi-level relationships
- Department and cost center hierarchy for expense allocation
- Base repository and service infrastructure for backoffice operations

## Requirements Addressed

**Functional Requirements:**
- FR-BO-001: Manage organizational structure (companies, branches, departments, cost centers)
- FR-BO-004: Maintain company master data (registration, tax IDs, addresses, bank accounts)
- FR-BO-005: Manage branch/office hierarchy with multi-level relationships
- FR-BO-006: Support department and cost center hierarchy for expense allocation

**Business Rules:**
- BR-BO-004: Organizational entities with active transactions cannot be deleted

**Performance:**
- PR-BO-001: Organizational hierarchy queries must complete in < 100ms for 1000+ entities

**Architecture:**
- ARCH-BO-001: Use nested set model or closure table for efficient hierarchy queries

**Security:**
- SR-BO-002: Log all administrative actions

**Integration:**
- IR-BO-002: Provide organizational hierarchy API for authorization and reporting
- IR-BO-003: Integrate with HCM for employee-department assignments

## Implementation Goals

### ✅ GOAL-001: Company Master Data Management
**Tasks:** [TASK-1.1 to TASK-1.18](https://github.com/azaharizaman/laravel-erp/blob/main/docs/plan/PRD01-SUB15-PLAN01-implement-organizational-foundation.md#goal-1-company-master-data-management)
- Company database schema with tenant isolation
- Company model with activity logging and soft deletes
- Company repository with contract interface
- Create/Update/Delete company actions with validation
- Company policy for authorization
- Company REST API controller
- Form requests and API resources
- Unit and feature tests (18 tests)

### ✅ GOAL-002: Organizational Hierarchy with Closure Table
**Tasks:** [TASK-2.1 to TASK-2.27](https://github.com/azaharizaman/laravel-erp/blob/main/docs/plan/PRD01-SUB15-PLAN01-implement-organizational-foundation.md#goal-2-organizational-hierarchy-with-closure-table)
- Organizations table (branch, department, cost_center types)
- Organization hierarchy closure table for efficient queries
- Organization model with parent-child relationships
- OrganizationHierarchyService for tree operations
- Organization repository with hierarchy queries
- Create/Update/Move/Delete organization actions
- Organization REST API with hierarchy endpoints
- Unit, feature, and performance tests (27 tests)

### ✅ GOAL-003: Repository & Service Infrastructure
**Tasks:** [TASK-3.1 to TASK-3.13](https://github.com/azaharizaman/laravel-erp/blob/main/docs/plan/PRD01-SUB15-PLAN01-implement-organizational-foundation.md#goal-3-repository--service-infrastructure)
- BackofficeServiceProvider with bindings
- Base service, policy, request, and resource classes
- Configuration file for cache TTL and hierarchy settings
- HasOrganization trait for models
- ValidateBackofficeAccess middleware
- API routes registration
- Package README and composer.json
- Unit and feature tests (13 tests)

### ✅ GOAL-004: Integration with Core Modules
**Tasks:** [TASK-4.1 to TASK-4.12](https://github.com/azaharizaman/laravel-erp/blob/main/docs/plan/PRD01-SUB15-PLAN01-implement-organizational-foundation.md#goal-4-integration-with-core-modules)
- InitializeTenantBackofficeListener (creates default company)
- OrganizationQueryService for user access validation
- User access API endpoint
- Employee-organization sync listener
- Helper functions for hierarchy navigation
- BackofficeSeeder for development data
- API documentation
- Integration and feature tests (12 tests)

### ✅ GOAL-005: Testing, Documentation & Deployment
**Tasks:** [TASK-5.1 to TASK-5.18](https://github.com/azaharizaman/laravel-erp/blob/main/docs/plan/PRD01-SUB15-PLAN01-implement-organizational-foundation.md#goal-5-testing-documentation--deployment)
- Comprehensive unit tests (all models, actions, services)
- Feature tests (complete API workflows)
- Integration tests (cross-module integration)
- Performance test (10,000 organizations, < 100ms queries)
- Pest configuration and 80% code coverage
- Migration guide, API documentation, admin guide
- CHANGELOG and version tagging
- Code review and staging deployment

## Technical Architecture

**Patterns:**
- Repository Pattern with contracts
- Laravel Actions (AsAction trait)
- Observer Pattern for model lifecycle
- Closure Table for hie

Adjacency list vs. nested sets: MySQL at EXPLAIN EXTENDED
records.body:
Adjacency list vs. nested sets: MySQL at EXPLAIN EXTENDED

https://ift.tt/33BCZeS

About 0 Minutes

Continuing the series:

What is better to store hierarchical data: nested sets model or adjacency list (parent-child) model?

For detailed explanations of the terms, see the first article in the series:

  • Adjacency list vs. nested sets: PostgreSQL

This is the last article of the series which covers MySQL.

MySQL differs from the other systems, since it is the only system of the big four that does not support recursion natively. It has neither recursive CTE's nor CONNECT BY clause, not even rowset returning functions that help to emulate recursion in PostgreSQL 8.3.

MySQL supports a thing that all other systems either lack or implement inefficiently: session variables. They can be set in a SELECT clause and can be used to keep some kind of a state between the rows as they are processed and returned in a rowset.

This of course is against the whole spirit of SQL, since SQL implies operations on whole sets and session variables operate on rows and are totally dependent on the order they are returned or processed. But if used properly, this behavior can be exploited to emulate some things that MySQL lacks: analytic functions, efficient random row sampling etc.

Hierarchical functions are among the things that need to be emulated in MySQL using session variables to keep the function state.

Here's the old article in my blog that shows how to do this:

  • Hierarchical queries in MySQL

On the other hand, MySQL implements one more thing that is useful for nested sets model: SPATIAL indexes.

Spatial indexes and nested sets model

Unlike most other systems, MySQL allows creating indexes of different types, one of them being SPATIAL.

A spatial index is an R-Tree structure that allows indexing multidimensional values (though MySQL only indexes two-dimensional ones). Each value is represented by its minimal bounding box (minimal rectangle that contains the whole shape), and this is what is stored in the index.

The index allows to find an answer efficiently to the following question: given a point, what are the boxes that contain it?

Though this type of query is commonly used on geometrical or geographical data, like find all public toilets within 100 meters of my current location and for God's sake don't make it a fullscan. However, this index can be used on any type of query that requires searching a given point in a range defined by two columns just as well.

A plain B-Tree index is good for range queries: find all values within the range defined by two boundaries, like shown on this picture:

Black dots show values that fall inside the range (defined with two constant boundaries). It's easy to find these values if they are sorted: all values will make a contiguous block. That's what exactly the B-Tree index do: sort the values and return contiguous blocks.
